# Volume 3 — Chapter XI The Round of Life

!!! note "Source text"
    Passages cited on the wiki pages link into this page. Only volumes at or before
    this page's cutoff are present.

Nell had returned to Brierley, bearing the prestige of the Thorburn Scholarship upon her forehead. She was informed by locals that she was largely unaltered, spoken with an inflection implying astonishment and mild chagrin that she remained the same. Brierley itself had likewise undergone no transformation. Such was her initial impression, at any rate. Yet, as Nell occupied the Grey Shutters pew during the initial Sunday following her arrival and surveyed the gathered people, she noticed various small alterations that, striking her simultaneously, forced her to understand that time was not entirely frozen, even within Brierley. The pulpit was occupied by a different minister. Within the pews, several accustomed faces had vanished permanently. Aged “Uncle Zeb,” whose predictions were now ended, Mrs. Peter Mott, who had uttered her final sigh, one hoped, Timothy Cotton, who, according to Mrs. Agatha Sowerby “had actually managed to die at last after practicing at it for twenty years,” alongside aged Josiah Mott, unrecognizable to everyone in his casket owing to his neatly groomed whiskers, were all buried in the small churchyard behind the building. Furthermore, Barney Pullen had taken Nettie Scobie as his wife! Their “appearing out” occurred that very Sunday. As Barney, glowing with satisfaction and joy, escorted his bride, dressed in feathers and silk, into the Gorham Pullen pew, Nell lowered her eyes to conceal her amused gaze. Her memory returned to the tempestuous winter evening during the Christmas vacation when Odette had made the marriage proposal on Barney’s behalf. His heart had clearly not been shattered by that refusal. Nell questioned whether Odette had likewise proposed to Nettie on his behalf, or whether he had summoned sufficient courage to pose the decisive question on his own. Every member of the Pullen family appeared to participate in his satisfaction and joy, extending from Mrs. Gorham seated in the pew to Odette singing in the choir. Odette had surrendered her position at the Brierley school and planned to travel West during the autumn.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0000 }

“Is unable to secure a suitor in Brierley, that is the reason,” stated Mrs. Agatha Sowerby with disdain. “Claims she believes her wellbeing will improve out West. It was never my understanding that her wellbeing was frail previously.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0001 }

“A sweet girl, Odette,” Nell had faithfully remarked. “Unlike certain others, she did not ever seek to draw eyes to herself.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0002 }

“Oh, if you are asking whether she pursued the boys, she certainly did not,” Mrs. Agatha remarked. “However, she harbored a desire to get married, precisely like anyone else, and that is the truth. What other reason could drive her to the West to a deserted spot that possesses no merit except a high population of men and a shortage of women? Do not attempt to convince me otherwise!”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0003 }

However, it was not toward Odette that Nell looked with distress and astonishment on that occasion. Instead, her eyes were fixed on Opal Pettigrew, who was seated next to her among the singers. What could have occurred to Opal? Although she had grown still more beautiful, her blue eyes shone with an overly vivid radiance, and her cheeks bore a feverishly intense flush; furthermore, she had become extremely slender, and the hands gripping her hymnal appeared nearly see-through in their fragility.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0004 }

“Has Opal Pettigrew taken sick?” inquired Nell to Mrs. Sowerby while the pair returned from the chapel.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0005 }

“Opal Pettigrew is dying of galloping consumption,” Mrs. Sowerby stated without preamble. “All the townspeople are aware of it, apart from her and her own kin. They refuse to admit it. According to them, her health is completely fine. Ever since her bout of congestion during the winter, she has been unable to instruct her classes, yet she claims she will resume teaching come autumn, and she is trying to secure the position at Pale Sands school. By the time the Pale Sands school term begins, that unfortunate girl will be lying in her grave, mark my words.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0006 }

Nell stood frozen in mute astonishment upon hearing the news. Was it really true that her former classmate, Opal Pettigrew, was on her deathbed? Though time had weakened their connection in recent years, the former bond of childhood friendship remained, striking Nell with a sudden, poignant ache. How could someone as radiant, lively, and teasing as Opal be linked to the grim reality of dying? Just after the church service, she had warmly and cheerfully welcomed Nell, insisting that she visit her the following night.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0007 }

“I will not be here Tuesday or Wednesday nights,” she had uttered in triumph. “A concert is taking place in Delford, followed by a gathering at Pale Sands. Herb Tranter is escorting me. He is my newest flame. Do not fail to visit me tomorrow. I am eager to have a proper conversation with you. I wish to know everything regarding your activities in Wexcombe.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0008 }

Nell was aware that Opal intended to inform Nell completely regarding her personal recent flirtations, yet she agreed to attend, and Isolde volunteered to accompany her.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0009 }

“For a long time I’ve been wishing to visit Opal,” she remarked to Nell, as they departed Grey Shutters the following evening, “yet I truly was unable to go by myself. Listening to Opal talk endlessly in that way of hers is so terrible, and her acting like she isn’t ill, even though coughing makes it nearly impossible for her to talk. She is striving so desperately to survive, and still, people claim she stands no possibility whatsoever.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0010 }

In silence, the girls journeyed along the red road at twilight. High up in the crowns of the trees, robins sang their evening prayers, pouring their joyous songs into the golden air. From the ponds and marshes, the silver piping of frogs drifted across the fields, where underground seeds started to awaken and react to the rain and sunlight that had passed above. A wild, sweet, and healthy scent wafted from patches of young raspberries, perfoming the air. Above quiet hollows, white fogs drifted, while blue-glowing violet stars illuminated the land around the brook.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0011 }

“What a lovely sunset,” Isolde remarked. “Look, Nell, it resembles a country all on its own, doesn’t it? That extended, low strip of purple cloud represents the coastline, and the bright sky beyond it is akin to a golden sea.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0012 }

“How wonderful it would be if we could journey there aboard the moonshine boat that Cedric mentioned in his former essay—do you recall it?” asked Nell, awakening from her musings. “Isolde, do you suppose all our yesterdays might be discovered in that place—every one of our former springs and blooms? Could the floral beds Cedric witnessed over there be the very roses that blossomed for us in days gone by?”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0013 }

“Stop!” Isolde said. “You cause me to feel as though we are elderly women with all of life already past.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0014 }

“Ever since I learned about poor Opal, I’ve felt nearly as though we were,” Nell said. “Any other mournful event could also be real if her impending death is indeed true.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0015 }

“Is it all right if we stop by Elisha Duckett’s briefly?” Isolde inquired. “I was requested by Mother to drop off this small bowl of jelly for Aunt Drusilla.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0016 }

“Which person is Aunt Drusilla?”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0017 }

“Ah, is this news to you? She is Tullyvale’s Mrs. Samson Coates, who happens to be Mrs. Elisha Duckett’s aunt. Furthermore, she is also my father’s aunt. Following the death of her husband this past winter, which left her in great poverty and solitude, the Ducketts welcomed her into their home. Although mother believed it was our duty to house her, father firmly refused. Under no circumstances would he reside alongside Aunt Drusilla.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0018 }

“Is she that awful?” Nell asked distractedly.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0019 }

“It is likely you will observe her true nature prior to our departure,” Isolde remarked meaningfully. “According to Father, her face resembles a hatchet that slices through the air. Nevertheless, her tongue possesses an even greater sharpness.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0020 }

Even though it was late, Aunt Drusilla sat in the Duckett kitchen cutting potato sets. Wearing a washed-out old wrapper, she had hair that was gray and unmistakably messy. Because Aunt Drusilla disliked being “caught in a kilter,” she made a special effort to be unpleasant.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0021 }

“Oh, so you’re Nell Harcourt?” she remarked, as Isolde presented Nell to her. “I’ve heard of you.” Her manner suggested that what she had heard was far from favorable. “Mrs. Pullen mentioned to me that you were back. She noted that you had gotten much better.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0022 }

It was beyond question that Aunt Drusilla believed there remained ample space for additional refinement. Without pause, she continued to sever acquaintanceships with great vigor.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0023 }

“Would there be any point in inviting you to take a seat?” she asked with sarcasm. “Naturally, you won't find much to amuse you here. Everyone else has gone out.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0024 }

“You were sent this small jar of rhubarb jelly by Mother,” Isolde remarked in an agreeable manner. “Having prepared it today, she believed you could enjoy a bit.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0025 }

“Oh, thank you,” Aunt Drusilla remarked with bitterness. “Your mother’s jelly has never appealed to me, as her recipe is always overly sweet. All the same, I shall attempt to force a little of it down. This spring, my eating has been terribly poor. My health is quite poor,” Aunt Drusilla added with gravity, “yet I carry on regardless. This world has no place for those who are unable to labor. Should it not prove overly burdensome, would you deign to place the jelly inside the pantry? Finishing these potatoes this evening is an urgent matter for me. I imagine that a pair of ladies such as yourselves would never engage in such tasks. The risk of ruining your hands would surely terrify you.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0026 }

“Prior to us renting the farm, I would slice potato sets,” Nell stated with a smile.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0027 }

“I still do that,” Isolde said with a laugh. “Last week, I skipped sets three days. Naturally,” she remarked in a teasing manner, “I put lemon juice and kid gloves on my hands every night following it.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0028 }

Aunt Drusilla let out a sniff.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0029 }

“My guess is that you derived that idea from one of those foolish periodicals you spend so much time reading. It surprises me that your mother permits it. However, you were always indulged by her. At the time Laurence wed her, every one of us believed she would prove to be an inappropriate spouse for him.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0030 }

Aunt Drusilla let out a deep sigh, as though every ominous prediction regarding Laurence Pembroke’s wedding had come to pass completely and gloomily.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0031 }

“Are you leaving?” she asked when the girls got up. “Well, talking to an old woman such as myself probably doesn't offer you much entertainment, I reckon. It is a shame that the boys are not at home.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0032 }

“We desire to pop inside and visit with Opal Pettigrew for a short time,” Isolde clarified.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0033 }

“Oh, naturally, any reason will suffice,” Aunt Drusilla remarked pleasantly. “Merely darting inside and darting back out prior to having a moment to offer a proper greeting. I reckon it is college pretentiousness. Staying clear of Opal Pettigrew would be more prudent for you. According to the doctors, consumption is contagious. I was certain Opal would contract a disease, running around visiting Boston this past autumn. Individuals who lack the contentment to remain at home invariably contract a disease.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0034 }

“Individuals who refrain from making calls contract illnesses as well. On occasion, they even perish,” Isolde remarked gravely.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0035 }

“They cannot hold themselves responsible for it in that case,” Aunt Drusilla answered with a victorious air. “Word has reached me that your wedding will take place in June, Isolde.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0036 }

“That rumor is completely false,” Isolde said, turning red.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0037 }

“Well, do not delay it for too long,” Aunt Drusilla remarked meaningfully. “You will lose your looks shortly—you consist entirely of complexion and hair. Furthermore, the Ducketts are exceedingly changeable. A hat should be worn by you, Miss Harcourt. Your nose is becoming scandalously freckled. My, what red hair you have! Ah well, I suppose we are all just as the Lord created us! Pass along my regards to Thirza Abernethy. She has not visited me a single time since I arrived in Brierley, though I imagine I should not protest. The Abernethys constantly believed they were superior to everybody else in these parts.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0038 }

“Oh, isn’t she terrible?” Isolde gasped, while they fled down the lane.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0039 }

“She is inferior to Miss Eliza Pullen,” Nell stated. “However, consider spending a lifetime bearing a moniker such as Drusilla! Is there anyone whose disposition it would not embitter? Her effort should have been directed toward conceiving her name to be Lucinda. A vast benefit could have been derived from that. That method assuredly aided me during the time I harbored a dislike for Nell.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0040 }

“Once Flossie Tulk reaches adulthood, she will resemble her completely,” Isolde remarked. “You are aware that Aunt Drusilla and Flossie’s mother are cousins, aren’t you? Ah, me, I am relieved that it has ended. She possesses such malice—a bitter taste seems to be added to everything by her. A remarkably amusing tale concerning her is told by Father. At one point, a clergyman who was exceptionally pious and decent, yet exceedingly hard of hearing, served in Tullyvale. No normal speech could be perceived by him whatsoever. Now, a prayer gathering was customarily held on Sunday nights, during which every member of the congregation in attendance would stand up to offer a prayer one by one, or speak briefly regarding a passage of scripture. On one particular night, however, Aunt Drusilla sprang to her feet. Neither a prayer nor a sermon was delivered by her. Rather, she attacked all the other people in the congregation and subjected them to a terrible tongue-lashing, identifying them explicitly by name, detailing the way every one of them had acted, and bringing back up every single feud and disgrace from the preceding decade. At last, she concluded by declaring that she felt revulsion toward the congregation at Tullyvale, that entering its portal ever again was far from her intentions, and that she trusted a terrible punishment would fall upon it. Exhausted, she then resumed her seat, and the clergyman, who had failed to catch a single statement she uttered, promptly observed, using a most pious tone, ‘amen! May the prayer of our beloved sister be granted by the Lord!’ The tale should be heard as told by Father.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0041 }

“Talking about tales, Isolde,” observed Nell, using a meaningful, secretive voice, “are you aware that recently I have been asking myself whether I might compose a short piece of fiction—a tale that would possess sufficient quality to get into print?”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0042 }

“Why, to be sure you were able to,” Isolde uttered, once she had comprehended the astonishing proposal. “You were accustomed to composing entirely exciting tales a long time back in our former Story Club.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0043 }

“Well, I scarcely intended that sort of tale,” Nell smiled. “I have pondered it somewhat recently, yet I am nearly fearful of attempting it, because, were I to be unsuccessful, the shame would be unbearable.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0044 }

“Honora mentioned to me on one occasion that every initial tale by Mrs. Varley was turned down. Nevertheless, I am certain that yours would avoid such a fate, Nell, since it is probable that modern editors possess greater judgment.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0045 }

“A story was written last winter by Margaret Burton, a Junior girl at Wexcombe, and Canadian Woman published it. Writing one that is at least as good is something I truly believe I could do.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0046 }

“And do you intend to publish it within the Canadian Woman?”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0047 }

“First, I could attempt to send it to a larger magazine. It hinges entirely on the type of story I produce.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0048 }

“What will the subject be?”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0049 }

“I am not sure so far. My goal is to secure a strong plot. From the perspective of an editor, I consider this extremely essential. The heroine’s name represents the single element I have determined. Evadne Garth shall be her name. Is it not quite lovely, in your opinion? Keep this secret from everyone, Isolde. Besides you and Mr. Pettifer, I have informed no one else. His reaction lacked encouragement—he claimed that an excess of rubbish was being produced these days already, and that he had anticipated a superior effort from me, following one year of college.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0050 }

“How can Mr. Pettifer know anything regarding that?” Isolde asked in a contemptuous tone.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0051 }

They discovered that the Pettigrew house was bright with illumination and visitors. From opposite sides of the parlor, Leonard Kimball, coming from Tullyvale, and Varley Bell, hailing from Delford, exchanged fierce looks. A number of cheerful young women had stopped by. Opal wore a white dress, and a strong luster marked both her eyes and her cheeks. She giggled and talked without stopping, and when the remaining girls departed, she escorted Nell to the upper floor so she could show off her recent summer gowns.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0052 }

“I still have a blue silk that needs to be made up, though it is rather heavy for the summer months, so I believe I will hold off on it until autumn. As you are aware, I am planning to teach at Pale Sands. What is your opinion of my hat? The one you wore to church yesterday was truly cute, but my preference is for something more vibrant. Have you seen those two foolish boys on the ground floor? Both of them arrived resolved to outstay the other. You know, I do not care even a little about any of them. Herb Tranter is the person I actually favor, and on occasion, I honestly believe he is the one for me. Back at Christmas, I believed the Tullyvale schoolmaster was that man, but I discovered something regarding him that made me lose interest. When I rejected him, he almost lost his mind. I really wish those two boys had stayed away tonight, because I was hoping we could have a wonderful, long conversation, Nell, so I could share so many things with you. The two of us have always been great friends, haven’t we?”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0053 }

With a slight, quiet chuckle, Opal encircled Nell’s waist with her arm. Yet their gaze locked for merely an instant, and within the depth of Opal’s shining eyes, Nell perceived a look that grieved her heart.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0054 }

“Will you come up frequently, Nell?” Opal murmured. “Make sure to come by yourself—I need you.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0055 }

“Is your health completely fine, Opal?”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0056 }

“Me! Well, I am completely fine. Never in my entire existence have I felt superior to this. To be sure, I was somewhat weakened by that congestion during the previous winter. However, simply look at my complexion. Surely, I do not appear at all like a sick person.”
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0057 }

With a tone that bordered on harshness, Opal spoke. Resentfully, it seemed, she jerked her arm from Nell and dashed down the stairs, becoming even more exuberant there, seemingly so captivated by teasing her pair of suitors that Nell and Isolde felt somewhat excluded and departed before long.
{: #nw-v03-c11-p0058 }
